Your assets/b2 idea is workable, but the key design choice is how each garden’s notes refer to assets. A mounted directory can make remote files feel local in Logseq; it does not, by itself, make those links work in a fresh Git checkout or on a published page.

Use separate buckets for public and private assets. Backblaze’s public setting permits anyone to download objects in the bucket, so a private prefix inside a public bucket would not protect private garden files. Your answer that private assets are for your authenticated devices only points to a private bucket and local paths, with no public CDN URL for those notes. The existing encode-garden bucket may serve the public side once its settings and key scope are verified. Backblaze bucket access settings

I would treat assets/b2 as a local view, not the whole storage design. rclone mount could put a B2 path there, but Logseq then depends on the mount process and network access; an ignored mount directory will be absent from another checkout. For private assets, a mise task that downloads files into assets/b2 may be more dependable, especially if you want notes readable offline. A mount remains a useful option if online access is acceptable. rclone mount documentation

The mount sounds like the right first local editing experience. The unresolved part is what a note's ../assets/b2/... link means when the mount is absent: on another device, in an agent's checkout, on GitHub, and in the published garden. A publishing task can translate the link, but the raw Markdown on GitHub would still point to a missing local file.

The translation itself does not need a secret. A documented object-path convention or a Git-tracked manifest can map a relative path to a public CDN URL. Uploading or checking a nonpublic B2 object needs credentials. CI should receive a narrowly scoped key for those operations; the local 1Password/Environment is not automatically available in CI.

To make this safe for agents away from the Mac, use the same mise entry points in every checkout. An asset task should check that the file or remote object exists, upload when authorized, and produce the exact Logseq link and public URL. A publish check should fail on unresolved assets/b2 links. An agent without the mount or upload credentials should be able to edit notes, but should not create a link that silently breaks on publication.

A bucket per garden is a good default when its audience and ownership are distinct: the existing encode-garden bucket can also hold Gitpa media under a podcast prefix if its public access is configured appropriately, while the private garden needs a separate private bucket for assets available only to authenticated devices. Confirm the existing bucket's visibility and key scope before reusing it. A rclone/remote names a connection and credential scope; it need not have the same name as the bucket or repo. dvc is worth a separate experiment if versioned binary inputs and repeatable conversions become central. Its .dvc files and lockfiles can record content hashes and pipeline dependencies, and Backblaze offers an S3-compatible endpoint for a DVC remote. DVC's content-addressed storage still needs a publishing step that copies selected outputs to stable, readable CDN object paths. It would not remove the link-translation problem. AI/Response I overweighted accidental deletion. The specific case is a writable mount turning an ordinary rm or mv into B2 operations. B2 has no atomic file rename, so moves can become copy then delete; the current log: config also has hard_delete=true, which permanently removes files on deletion instead of retaining a hidden version. That is a recovery hazard, but a read-only mount would obstruct the file organization you expect. A bucket-scoped key that permits normal moves, hard_delete=false, a sensible version-retention policy, and a separately tested backup are better controls if a writable mount proves useful. rclone move, rclone B2 versions and hard delete, Backblaze file versions

The 1Password names now reflect the two roles. Backblaze administration retains the existing account-wide key and its local .env mount. logseq-encode-publishing exists but has no variables or mount yet. The current rclone wrapper still reads the old mount path, so the two roles are not operationally separated until a bucket-scoped key is created and the wrapper is switched.

The concern about a read-only mount is fair. The real requirement is that an agent can author a public page from another checkout without this Mac's mount. A stable URL on a media domain you control lets Logseq, GitHub, CI, and remote agents read an existing public asset directly. A local mount or downloaded copy can remain an optional editing convenience. For newly created remote assets, an agent needs a scoped upload path; otherwise the page should use an existing URL or an asset committed to Git until upload is available. This is a design proposal, pending the choice between source URLs and relative links above.

rclone mount presents B2 as a filesystem, but a remote file read may fetch data on a cache miss, and directory access may require remote listing. The number of B2 requests depends on rclone's VFS and directory caches; a filesystem read is not always one B2 request. At current Backblaze pay-as-you-go pricing, Class A/B/C API calls are free, while direct downloads count against the included egress of 3× average monthly storage before overage charges. The larger practical costs for this workflow may be latency, offline failure, and sandbox access to FUSE or credentials. Measure a small mount pilot before depending on it. rclone mount and VFS cache, Backblaze transaction pricing, Backblaze B2 pricing
